Frequently Asked Questions

Everything you need to know about registering a One-Person Company in Suzhou Industrial Park. Can't find what you're looking for? Contact us anytime.

Yes. In Suzhou Industrial Park (SIP), foreigners can register a 100% foreign-owned One-Person Company. No Chinese partner, sponsor, or local shareholder is required.

This is one of the key advantages of the OPC structure in SIP — it was specifically designed to encourage foreign entrepreneurship. You maintain full ownership and control of your company.

You will need the following documents:

  • Valid passport (with sufficient remaining validity)
  • Proposed company name (in Chinese and English)
  • Business scope description
  • Registered address proof (we can provide this)
  • Proof of residential address from your home country
  • Notarized and authenticated copies of overseas documents

We handle the notarization and authentication process for you, so you don't need to worry about the paperwork logistics.

The total cost depends on your specific needs, but here's a general breakdown:

  • Government fees: Approximately 500–1,000 RMB (nominal)
  • Company seal & chops: 300–600 RMB
  • Registered address (annual): Starting from 6,000 RMB/year
  • Our service fee: Contact us for a tailored quote
  • Bank account opening: Typically free with partner banks

Unlike WFOE registration, there is no minimum capital requirement, so your upfront investment can be as low as you choose.

With our guidance, the full registration process typically takes 15–20 working days from the moment we receive your documents:

  • Days 1–3: Name pre-approval and document preparation
  • Days 4–8: Business license application and processing
  • Days 9–12: Company seals (chops) and bank account opening
  • Days 13–20: Tax registration and final compliance setup

Timelines may vary slightly depending on document authentication times and bank processing.

No, you do not need to be in China during the registration process. We can handle the entire setup remotely using notarized and authenticated documents from your home country.

However, you will need to visit China in person when:

  • Opening the corporate bank account (most banks require in-person verification)
  • Applying for a work permit and residence permit (if you plan to live in China)
  • Collecting the original business license and company seals (we can courier these if needed)

We can coordinate with you to schedule these visits efficiently, minimizing your time in China.

While both allow 100% foreign ownership, there are key differences:

  • Shareholders: An OPC has exactly one shareholder; a WFOE can have multiple.
  • Capital: OPCs have no minimum capital; WFOEs often require significant registered capital.
  • Setup time: OPCs take 15–20 days; WFOEs typically take 2–3 months.
  • Compliance: OPCs have simpler reporting; WFOEs have more extensive requirements.
  • Best for: OPCs suit solo entrepreneurs; WFOEs suit larger operations.

Your OPC can later be converted into a multi-shareholder company or WFOE as your business grows.

Yes. Once your OPC is registered and has a corporate bank account, you can hire both Chinese and foreign employees. You will need to:

  • Open social insurance and housing fund accounts
  • Sign labor contracts compliant with Chinese labor law
  • Withhold and pay individual income tax (IIT) on behalf of employees
  • For foreign employees: sponsor work permits and residence permits

We offer full HR and payroll services to manage this for you, so you can focus on growing your business.

An OPC can operate in most industries, including but not limited to:

  • Consulting and professional services
  • Technology and software development
  • E-commerce and trading
  • Design, media, and creative services
  • Import/export (with appropriate licenses)
  • Education and training services

Certain restricted industries (such as finance, telecommunications, and media broadcasting) may have additional requirements or limitations. We'll help you define a business scope that fits your plans while staying compliant.

After your OPC is registered, you'll need to maintain the following compliance obligations:

  • Annual report: File an annual enterprise report with the local administration
  • Tax filing: Monthly or quarterly tax declarations (even if zero)
  • Bookkeeping: Maintain proper accounting records per Chinese standards
  • Audit: Annual financial audit (required for most companies)
  • Social insurance: Monthly contributions if you have employees

Our ongoing compliance packages start from 800 RMB/month and cover all of the above, so you never miss a deadline.

Not if you are the sole owner with no employees. In China, social insurance is mandatory for employees, but as a foreign founder and sole shareholder of an OPC, you are not required to enroll yourself. The notice is an automated message sent to all newly registered companies.

Here is what you need to know:

  • Sole owner (yourself): Not mandatory. You may voluntarily enroll if you choose to, but this is uncommon among foreign entrepreneurs in China
  • Employees: Mandatory once you hire your first employee. Your accountant will handle the corporate account opening and monthly contributions
  • The notice: A standard automated reminder from the Social Insurance Center. If you have no employees, you can safely ignore it

Your accountant will alert you when employee enrollment is required and handle the paperwork for you.

Yes, absolutely. The OPC is designed as a starting point, not a permanent state. As your business grows, you can:

  • Add shareholders: Convert from a one-person company to a multi-shareholder limited liability company (LLC)
  • Convert to WFOE: If you need to scale significantly, the structure can be reorganized
  • Attract investment: Bring in investors by issuing new shares
  • Establish branches: Open branch offices in other Chinese cities

The conversion process is straightforward and typically takes 2–4 weeks. We handle the entire transition so your business operations continue uninterrupted.

An OPC is a formal legal entity; freelancing is not. Here are the key differences:

  • Legal status: An OPC has a business license and is recognized by the government; freelancers operate as individuals without a registered entity
  • Contracts: An OPC can sign contracts, issue official invoices (fapiao), and open corporate bank accounts; freelancers cannot
  • Liability: An OPC provides limited liability protection; freelancers bear unlimited personal liability
  • Credibility: Clients trust licensed companies more than individual freelancers, especially for larger projects
  • Visa support: An OPC can sponsor work permits and residence permits; freelancing alone cannot

If you are already freelancing, registering an OPC is the natural next step to professionalize your business and unlock new opportunities.

OPCs are ideal for solo entrepreneurs who want a lightweight, legitimate business structure. Typical OPC founders include:

  • Consultants and advisors: Business, legal, marketing, or technical consultants serving clients in China
  • Developers and designers: Software engineers, UI/UX designers, and creative professionals
  • Content creators: Writers, videographers, and media professionals building a brand
  • Traders and agents: Import/export agents and sourcing professionals
  • AI-powered solopreneurs: Entrepreneurs leveraging AI tools to run a one-person operation at scale

If you have a skill, a network, and the ambition to build something of your own, an OPC is likely the right fit.

The single biggest legal risk is asset commingling — mixing personal and company funds. In China, if a one-person company owner cannot clearly separate personal assets from company assets, courts can "pierce the corporate veil" and hold the owner personally liable for company debts.

To protect yourself:

  • Always use the corporate bank account for business transactions
  • Never pay personal expenses from the company account
  • Keep proper accounting records and receipts
  • Pay yourself a salary through payroll rather than random withdrawals

Our compliance packages include bookkeeping and financial oversight to help you maintain this separation from day one.

Once your OPC is registered, you can apply for an invoice (fapiao) quota from the tax bureau. The process works as follows:

  • Apply for invoice rights: Submit an application to the local tax office (we handle this)
  • Choose invoice type: VAT ordinary invoice (普通发票) or VAT special invoice (专用发票) depending on client needs
  • Issue online: Most invoices can be issued electronically through the tax bureau's online platform
  • Report taxes: Invoice amounts must be declared in your monthly or quarterly tax filing

We guide you through the entire invoicing setup and can even issue invoices on your behalf as part of our ongoing compliance service.

AI can boost a one-person company's efficiency by up to 300%. Here are the most useful categories of tools for OPC founders:

  • Content creation: ChatGPT, Claude, and Chinese models like Doubao and Kimi for writing, translation, and client communication
  • Design: Midjourney, DALL-E, and Canva AI for marketing materials and social media graphics
  • Code and automation: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and no-code tools like Zapier for building products and automating workflows
  • Customer service: AI chatbots for handling routine client inquiries 24/7
  • Data analysis: AI-powered analytics tools for understanding market trends and client behavior

As an AI-focused entrepreneurship community, Moon Bay OPC helps founders select and implement the right AI tools for their specific business model.

One of the biggest advantages of an OPC is that there is no minimum capital requirement. You can register with as little as 1 RMB of registered capital if you choose.

However, for practical business purposes, we recommend budgeting for:

  • Initial setup: 1,000–2,000 RMB (government fees, seals, basic services)
  • First year operating costs: 6,000–12,000 RMB (registered address, bookkeeping, compliance)
  • Living expenses: If you plan to move to China, budget for rent, food, and transport
  • Tools and software: AI subscriptions, domain names, hosting, etc.

Many successful OPC founders start with under 20,000 RMB in total first-year investment. The key is to start lean and reinvest revenue as you grow.

This is a rapidly evolving area. Under current Chinese copyright law, works must be created by a human to qualify for copyright protection. Purely AI-generated content without meaningful human input may not be copyrightable.

To protect your work:

  • Add substantial human creativity: Use AI as a starting point, then edit, refine, and add original elements
  • Document your creative process: Keep drafts showing your human contributions
  • Use clear contracts: Specify IP ownership in client agreements, especially for AI-assisted deliverables
  • Label AI-generated content: China's AI regulations require clear labeling of AI-generated content in certain contexts

We can connect you with IP lawyers who specialize in AI-related copyright questions to ensure your business is fully protected.

Suzhou Industrial Park offers several tax advantages for small businesses and startups:

  • Small-scale taxpayer status: If your annual revenue is under 5 million RMB, you qualify for reduced VAT rates (1% instead of 6% or 13%)
  • Income tax reductions: Qualified small and micro enterprises enjoy reduced corporate income tax rates
  • Startup subsidies: Certain industries and talent categories qualify for one-time grants
  • R&D deductions: If your OPC engages in research and development, you may qualify for additional tax deductions

Our tax consultants stay current on all SIP policies and will ensure you claim every incentive you are entitled to.
